90.0.s.en: (1) The eternal God and transient man

90.0.0.en: 1- Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.

90.0.1.en: 1- God is a refuge for the children of His people throughout the ages; when they meet various afflictions and trials, they hasten to Him, and He supports them. He kept them from the days of their father Abraham in the land of Canaan, then in Egypt, and brought them out and freed them from the bondage of Pharaoh with an uplifted arm, and drowned Pharaoh and all his army.

90.0.2.en: 2- When man becomes a stranger to the desires of the world, he is able to feel God, and hastens to Him as a refuge instead of the passing and changing things of the world. Then he experiences God's help, care and protection.

90.1.0.en: 2- Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

90.1.1.en: 1- God, who is a refuge for His people, is the One who created the whole world with its greatest things, that is, the high mountains, for He has existed from eternity, and He lives for ever, and He is steadfast and does not change throughout the generations.

90.1.2.en: 2- If God is steadfast and exists before all creatures, then He is the greatest refuge, and there is no other protection like Him; therefore His people live in tranquility with Him, and He will take them with Him for ever in the Kingdom.

90.2.0.en: 3- Thou turnest man to dust; and sayest, “Return, ye children of men.”

90.2.1.en: God's anger at man is because of man's separation from Him, when Adam and Eve fell, and by this man came down from his rank and became dust, that is, earth, and this is what God declared to man after his fall (Gen 3:19). But at the same time God gives man hope by calling him to return to Him by repentance, so that He may accept him and raise him to his first rank. And this shows the extent of God's compassion and longsuffering.

90.3.0.en: 4- For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.

90.3.1.en: 1- Even if the people of God live a thousand years in sin, God is longsuffering toward them, and when His people repent He rejoices in them, and even counts the thousand years as one day. And this shows God's longsuffering and His forgiveness of man.

90.3.2.en: 2- God shows His love in that He considers the period of His people's disobedience, even if it extended a thousand years, as a watch of the night, and the night is divided into four parts, so a watch is about three hours. God says this to confirm His love and forgiveness for His children however long they continue in their sins; what matters is that they return to Him by repentance, and He wipes the sin away from them as though it had not been.

90.4.0.en: 5- Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep: in the morning they are like grass which passeth away. 6- In the morning it flourisheth and passeth away; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth.

90.4.1.en: As a sleep: like slumber. Morning: the early morning

90.4.2.en: 1- He likens the life of man to being short and passing like a period of sleep and like a dream that man sees during the night and it ends quickly. Therefore man must hasten to repentance, and not be occupied with sins or the desires of the world, but renounce them in order to live for God.

90.4.3.en: 2- He also likens the life of man to grass that grows with vitality in the period of youth, then flowers in the period of manhood, but after this withers in the period of old age, which is referred to by the evening, and this grass is cut down and passes away. That is, however great man's life may appear, he is weak, so he should not be occupied with the prosperity and positions of the passing world, because all this is perishable, and man should live for God, and hasten always to repentance, and prepare for his eternity.

90.4.4.en: If our life is short and changing, and everything in the world is passing, then we ought to look to God, who is lasting and remains for ever, and from whom, through whom and for whom is our life. And if we sin, let us hasten to Him with repentance, for He is merciful and accepts us and brings us back to His arms, and we enjoy His love for ever.

90.5.s.en: (2) The wrath of God and the shortness of man's life

90.5.0.en: 7- For we are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled. 8- Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance.

90.5.1.en: 1- Moses comes forward on behalf of his people to offer repentance for them, and by this he pleads for the mercies of God, and implores Him because the people are in terror and almost perish from the wrath of God upon them, for they sinned and deserved punishment when they asked to return to Egypt instead of entering the land of Canaan, so God made them wander in the wilderness of Sinai forty years, so that all the adults would perish and only their sons would enter.

90.5.2.en: 2- What exposed the evil of the people before God was that God looked at them with His shining face, which uncovers secret things, even if they are not apparent to people, or even to the sinning man himself, for God reveals them, that man may repent of them.

90.5.3.en: 3- The light of God's countenance was completed in the incarnate Christ, who revealed the secret sins of men, and paid the debt for mankind and redeemed us on the Cross.

90.6.0.en: 9- For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told.

90.6.1.en: 1- Moses feels that God's wrath continued a long time upon his people, forty years, until all the days of those who came out of Egypt were ended, with God angry at them, and they all died in the wilderness; even Moses himself did not enter the Promised Land, but saw it from afar, and only the children entered, who grew up, and with them Joshua and Caleb, who obeyed God when they were sent to spy out the Promised Land.

90.6.2.en: 2- Moses shows that the life of man is short and limited, and he likens it to a story that is told, which has an end, and therefore man should not cling to earthly things, but renounce the world and look to God, to whom he will go and with whom he will live for ever.

90.7.0.en: 10- The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.

90.7.1.en: 1- Moses affirms that the life of man is short, for it generally does not exceed seventy years, and may reach eighty, and most people die before this age. And whatever the blessings of God to man, the pains of life do not leave him, from the toils of the body, diseases, and the various problems of life. And thus the life of man ends quickly, as straw flies with the wind.

90.7.2.en: 2- If Moses lived more than eighty years, for he lived a hundred and twenty years, this is a gift from God which He gives to some people to fulfill divine purposes, such as leading the people of God to the borders of the land of Canaan, and if life ends quickly for those who believe in God, their spirits fly and ascend to heaven.

90.8.0.en: 11- Who knoweth the power of thine anger? even according to thy fear, so is thy wrath.

90.8.1.en: 1- God's anger is very severe and frightening beyond all imagination, for if God is unlimited then His anger is also unlimited; therefore every person must think of God's anger when Satan tries to draw him into sin, so that he may quickly keep away from it.

90.8.2.en: 2- When man fell in the Garden of Eden, and his falls followed one another, God was very angry at Satan, and decided to become incarnate to redeem man and bring him back to His arms.

90.9.0.en: 12- So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

90.9.1.en: 1- If our days and their number are limited, that is, our life is short, then we should walk with care and wisdom. And this wisdom is not from the earth but from God; therefore Moses the prophet asks God to teach us wisdom so that we may walk well and keep away from sin, for the wise heart keeps away from sin because it lives with God.

90.9.2.en: 2- The heart of wisdom is feelings filled with wisdom, that we may live by them in the midst of our troubled world. And true wisdom is the most upright wisdom, that is, the incarnate Christ; this is what he asks of God, for Moses awaits in hope the Incarnation of Christ, who redeems mankind and gives it wisdom to walk in the way of the Kingdom.

90.9.3.en: I wish, my brother, that you would seize the opportunity of this short life to live with God and keep away from every sin, and let it not entice you with its beauty and its desire, for all this is passing, and what remains is God alone.

90.10.s.en: (3) Hope in the mercy of God

90.10.0.en: 13- Return, O Lord, how long? and let it repent thee concerning thy servants. 14- O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.

90.10.1.en: 1- Since life is short, all hope is in God. Therefore Moses the prophet calls on behalf of mankind, asking God to come quickly and have compassion on mankind, so that He redeems it from sin and satisfies it with His love, and He declares this early, that is, at the dawn of Sunday by His holy Resurrection.

90.10.2.en: 2- The Incarnation of Christ gladdens the hearts of all who believe in Him, not on earth only, but rather in heaven for ever.

90.11.0.en: 15- Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil.

90.11.1.en: 1- When we were immersed in sin God was angry and forsook us, so we were in great humiliation. But when we repent God compensates us for the humiliation of sin with great joy, which is a divine gift that God grants to His repentant servants, and they call on God and glorify Him. And their offspring also see it and continue to glorify Him and keep away from every sin.

90.11.2.en: 2- In order for us to repent and reject sin we need the work of God in us, so that He pricks us and convicts us to repent.

90.12.0.en: 17- And let the grace of the Lord our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it. At the close of the Psalm Moses the prophet asks that the grace of God come upon him and upon all who believe in God. And for the grace of God to come it is necessary for man to show his response to God by spiritual striving, which he repeated in this verse twice to confirm its importance. And he says “the work of our hands,” which is our striving, and by it he means love, whether the love of God or of others, so he does not say the works of our hands but the work of our hands, because love is the bond of perfection.

90.12.1.en: Whatever your sins, and however much the problems around you increase, do not be troubled, for God your Father sees you and hears your requests, and trust that He will intervene and give you rest, and even joy, and His grace will come upon you.

90.12.2.en: The shelter of the Most High. “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (v. 1). Introduction:

90.12.3.en: 1- Its writer is one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those for which no writer is mentioned, and some think its writer is David, and some that it is Moses, because it was placed in the order after Psalm ninety, which Moses the prophet wrote.

90.12.4.en: 2- This Psalm speaks about the power of God, His fatherhood, and His care for His children, so that they do not fear the wicked, because God rescues them from their hands, so it is a reassuring Psalm for the children of God; therefore many repeat it throughout their day.

90.12.5.en: 3- It is one of the Messianic Psalms, because it speaks about the life of Christ in His trials and sufferings, and indeed Satan quoted part of this Psalm (vv. 11, 12) (Mt 4:6) and Satan did not complete the Psalm, because it contains a prophecy about the crushing of Satan by the Cross (v. 13).

90.12.6.en: 4- The name of God is mentioned with four titles, to reassure His children in this Psalm, and they are (the Most High - the Almighty - God - the Lord).

90.12.7.en: 5- This Psalm is found in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ passed through the sufferings alone and crushed Satan by His Cross, because Christ was crucified in this hour.

91.0.s.en: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

91.0.0.en: 1- He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.

91.0.2.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm calls God the Most High because He is higher than all the powers of the world, so whoever takes refuge in His shelter and hides in it, no one can harm him. And he also calls Him the Almighty, because He is able to do all things, and no one can stand before Him.

91.0.3.en: 2- The children of God dwell between the hands of God, and also abide in His shadow, that is, His protection, so they settle reassured and are not disturbed by any turmoil in the world, that is, they continue in peace in the care of God.

91.0.4.en: 3- The shelter of the Most High, as St. Athanasius says, is the commandments of God, so whoever keeps them, God keeps him from all dangers.

91.1.0.en: 2- I will say of the Lord, “He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.”

91.1.1.en: 1- Because of the multitude of enemies the writer of the Psalm flees to God, who is a refuge and fortress for him, and he finds protection from all enemies however strong they may be.

91.1.2.en: 2- Because of the writer's confidence in God he trusts in Him, and does not trust in himself or in any other power in the world. And in order to trust in God he must be repentant and rejecting every sin, that is, walking uprightly, and then God accepts him and protects him. Just as the killer in the Old Testament used to take refuge in God, represented in the cities of refuge, on condition that the killing was unintentional, but if he was a deliberate killer the elders of the city of refuge did not accept him, and consequently whoever regards sin as permissible and clings to it, God does not accept him if he tries to take shelter in Him.

91.2.0.en: 3- Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence.

91.2.1.en: Pestilence: a disease that spreads quickly and infects people by contagion.

91.2.2.en: 1- The fowler is Satan and his snares are his tricks, deceit and thoughts, and all his evil works into which he makes men fall, but however great Satan's power, it is nothing before the power of God, who is able to deliver His children from all the snares of the demons, and uncovers the hidden snares, and gives discernment to His children, so that they keep away from every evil.

91.2.3.en: 2- The pestilence is sin, for it spreads quickly among people, and many fall into it, but God is also able to deliver His children from it, whether this sin is lusts, or heresies, or doubts, or anything that draws us away from God.

91.3.0.en: 4- He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.

91.3.1.en: His feathers: the small feathers found under the wings of a bird.

91.3.2.en: Buckler: the large shield, and the shield is a piece of wood with a handle at the back in which the soldier puts his hand and moves the shield in front of his head and body, to protect him from the arrows of the enemy.

91.3.3.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm likens God to a bird that has wings with large feathers, and under them small feathers with which it shades its young, as the eagle does, so God shades His children, and protects them from the blows of the enemy Satan, and becomes for them a refuge and fortress, and consequently they no longer fear Satan. And this is what Christ declared when He likened Himself to the hen that gathers her chicks and shades them with her wings (Lk 13:34), so the chicks are hidden from the face of the enemy and he does not snatch them.

91.3.4.en: 2- He also likens God to the shield and buckler with which the soldier protects himself, so God's truth, that is, everyone who believes in God, this faith becomes for him a shield that protects him from the thoughts of Satan and his snares.

91.4.0.en: 5- Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day;

91.4.2.en: 1- Whoever trusts in God is not disturbed by the wars of Satan that come in the night, and all the fears of that time, and what is meant by the night is the hidden wars concealed in the darkness, while the arrow that flies by day is the open wars, where Satan or the wicked appear and show their evil to the righteous man in order to harm him.

91.4.3.en: 2- He also adds regarding the wars of Satan that they spread quickly in the darkness, which represents obscurity and mystery; in addition to the wars of Satan at noonday, when man is occupied with food and rest, and Satan attacks him and destroys him because of his slackness and lack of attention, and this means that the wars of Satan are continuous night and day, so constant attention and watchfulness against them are necessary.

91.4.4.en: 3- These two verses declare God's continuous care for His children night and day, to protect them from all the wars of the devil, which reassures them and even encourages them to resist these wars and triumph over Satan.

91.5.0.en: 7- A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee.

91.5.1.en: Ten thousand: plural of ribwa, which is ten thousand.

91.5.2.en: 1- Since God protects His children who are joined to Him, He helps them in their striving, and strikes the demons who fight them, whether from the right side or from the other side, which is the left, so the demons cannot come near or defeat the children of God.

91.5.3.en: 2- The left side includes the wars of falling into various sins, when the spiritual man is in lukewarmness and weakness, and exposed to falling. As for the right, it represents the state of the spiritual man who is joined to God in spiritual practices, and thinks his state is good, though he is negligent in many matters, so more demons, whose number reaches tens of thousands, fight him to try to make him fall, and if they find him in a state of weakness and negligence he responds to the wars of the demons, but if he holds fast to his striving, then tens of thousands of satanic wars are worthless, and God protects him from them.

91.6.0.en: 8- Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold and see the reward of the wicked.

91.6.1.en: 1- God encourages His children, if afflictions meet them, to bear them, because in the end God will punish the wicked for all their sins, but His children He will justify.

91.6.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about what will happen on the Day of Judgment, for Christ in His first coming endured much injustice, and His children also endured toils and persecutions even to death, but Christ in His second coming will recompense all the wicked and cast them into eternal torment.

91.6.3.en: If you strive and bear the pains of striving and the afflictions from the wicked, do not be troubled by them because they are temporary; be confident of the righteousness in which you walk, but evil will not endure.

91.7.s.en: (2) The strength of the children of God

91.7.0.en: 9- Because thou hast said, “Thou, Lord, art my refuge.” Thou hast made the most High thy habitation;

91.7.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm addresses the righteous man, and says to him that you have declared that God is your refuge, then the writer of the Psalm continues his speech, and says to the righteous man that you have made God the Most High a dwelling for yourself. That is, the righteous man chose God as his refuge, and consequently no one can harm him, but he has settled and dwelt in God the Most High, who is above all, and no one can reach Him, so the righteous man is in complete protection.

91.7.2.en: 2- This verse is a confirmation of the meaning declared in (v. 2).

91.8.0.en: 10- There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling.

91.8.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm offers new promises to the righteous man, namely that no evil will meet him in his life; because God does not allow him anything that harms him, and turns evil into good; for all things work together for good to them that love God (Rom 8:28).

91.8.2.en: 2- Also a new promise he offers, which is that no plague will come near the tent of the righteous man, that is, his place of settlement and peace; for God may allow him a trial, but the plague is a punishment and harm that befalls man, and this does not happen to the righteous man, but he keeps his peace even within afflictions and trials. And that is because of his faith in God, which remains steadfast. For righteous Job was exposed to harsh trials and not plagues, so he learned and benefited from his trials, and remained with God, but what befell Pharaoh is called plagues and not trials, because they were a punishment for him, and a warning of the nearness of his destruction.

91.9.0.en: 11- For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. 12- They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.

91.9.1.en: 1- A new promise to the righteous man: that God sends His angels to keep him in all his ways; that is, the angels guard him at every step, and this is a clear scriptural declaration of the guardian angel who accompanies each one of the children of God.

91.9.2.en: 2- This verse shows the ministry of the angels to men (Heb 1:14), and indeed in their tenderness they bear up the righteous man so that he does not stumble by striking against any stone, that is, afflictions do not trouble him, but they lift him by the command of God above them, and by this his heart is lifted to heaven, and he feels God within the trial more than at any other time, and enjoys the company of the angels.

91.9.3.en: 3- Satan tried to use this verse in the temptation of Christ on the mountain, but Christ exposed his deceit and rejected the pride that Satan intended. And it is noticed that Satan did not complete the words of the Psalm (v. 13), which says “the lion and adder shalt thou tread upon,” because it declares that Christ will trample Satan, who is the lion and the adder (the serpent).

91.10.0.en: 13- Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the serpent shalt thou trample under feet.

91.10.1.en: The adder: a vicious kind of snake.

91.10.2.en: The young lion: the little lion.

91.10.3.en: 1- Another promise given to the righteous man, which is that he will tread upon, have dominion over, and triumph over Satan, who is symbolized by the lion and the young lion for his strength (1 Pet 5:8), and is also symbolized by snakes, that is, serpents, for their cunning (Lk 10:17-19).

91.10.4.en: 2- The authority that God gives to His children is over every sin, and He gives them power to reject sin, and if they fall into it they rise with hope, confident that with God they are stronger than the wars of the demons, and they are not troubled by the plots of the wicked; for God will bring them through all afflictions, and bring them in peace to the Kingdom.

91.11.0.en: 14- “Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name.

91.11.1.en: 1- God promises the righteous man who obeys His commandments that He will deliver him from any affliction, and lift him above the trial; because he clung to God, that is, was attached to Him and loved Him very much. And because he knew God closely, and realized that He is the only God able to satisfy all his needs, and because he knew the great God exalted above all creatures, so when the righteous man knows Him he rises to Him, and is lifted above material things.

91.11.2.en: 2- This divine promise is for the whole Church if she clings to Him and knows His name, for He delivers her and raises her to true spirituality, until He brings her to the heavenly Kingdom. For God will allow afflictions, but afterward He delivers her from them.

91.12.0.en: 15- He shall call upon me, and I will answer him: I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him, and honour him. 16- With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation.

91.12.1.en: 1- The righteous man who obeys God, if he takes refuge in Him and prays, God cares very much for his prayers and supplication, which come from his heart because he is in affliction, so He answers him, and rescues him from falling into sin, and indeed the righteous man experiences the fellowship of God, and enjoys Him, and receives the earnest of the Kingdom within the affliction, and rejoices. And by this God glorifies him in the midst of affliction, as He did with the three youths in the fiery furnace.

91.12.2.en: 2- After this God grants the righteous man who endured affliction and took refuge in God a grace than which no grace is greater, which is that He gives him long days without end, and complete salvation, in the heavenly Kingdom.

91.12.3.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ, who while crucified prayed to the Father, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46), and He answered Him and rescued Him and glorified Him by the Resurrection from the dead; then He ascended to the heavens, and prepared a place for all His children who believe in Him, who call on Him, and He answers them.

91.12.4.en: God awaits your prayers when any affliction comes upon you, in order to rescue you from it, and He gives you a peace that surpasses understanding, then brings you out of it, and rewards you with a great reward in the heavens for your endurance of the trial.

91.12.5.en: The greatness of those who praise God. “It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord ...” (v. 1)

91.12.8.en: The writer is not mentioned in the title, so it is considered one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those whose writer is unknown. But it is thought to be:

91.12.9.en: a - David the prophet, with the purpose that it be chanted on the Sabbath day in the temple.

91.12.12.en: After David triumphed over his enemies, and God gave him rest from wars, he wrote this Psalm to praise God.

91.12.13.en: 3- This Psalm used to be chanted by the Levites and the people on the Sabbath day inside the temple to glorify God, and by this it is understood that it is a liturgical Psalm offered in congregational worship.

91.12.14.en: 4- This Psalm shows the greatness of praise and the blessings of God to His righteous children, for it is thanksgiving to God, and at the same time an encouragement to a life of righteousness and keeping away from evil.

91.12.15.en: 5- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
